newsitem.title: UK: Nazis wiping out Jews sooner than thought - records.
newsitem.headline: Nazis wiping out Jews sooner than thought - records.

text.p: Nazi Germany's systematic bid to wipe out the Jews started shortly after the June 1941 invasion of Russia and not many months later as was first believed, according to intelligence documents released on Monday.
Transcripts of intercepted German police messages showed without doubt that the Allies suspected as early as September 1941 that the Nazis wanted to exterminate the Jews.
Around six million Jews are believed to have died in the Nazi Holocaust, which historians had originally believed was set in motion some time in early 1942.
But the German police messages -- intercepted and decoded by the Bletchley Park intelligence-gathering centre outside London -- seemed to tell a different story.
On September 12, 1941, British intelligence said that the execution of Jews was a recurrent feature of the reports sent by the German police.

"Whether those executed as 'Jews' are indeed such is of course doubtful; but the figures are no less conclusive as evidence of a policy of savage intimidation if not of ultimate extermination," it said.
Ordinary soldiers, SS special units and the Ordnungspolizei police, who kept order in the occupied territories, all took part in mass shootings of Jews.
Historians estimate that up to half a million Soviet Jews may have died at the hands of German troops in the months after the June 22, 1941 invasion.
The British report seemed to cast doubt on this figure, but said it was highly significant that the German forces were so keen to stress how many of their victims were Jews.
"Many, no doubt, were not Jews; but the fact that this heading invariably produced the biggest figures shows this is the ground for killing most acceptable to the higher authorities," it continued.

British intelligence said the Ordnungspolizei stopped sending details of executions by radio in mid-September 1941 after their commander Kurt Daluege, "alarmed perhaps by our evident awareness of the unspeakable activities of his police in Russia", said such information should only be passed on by special courier.
But some details slipped through under the the euphemistic title of "action according to the usage of war" and even after Daluege's order some still sent execution details by radio.

The early slaughter seems to have been particularly intense on the southern sector of the Russian front, where the Germans shot 12,361 Jews in the week of August 23 to 31. At least 3,353 Jews were executed in the first 13 days of September.
German commanders elsewhere sent in death tolls with the casual ease of rat-catchers.

"The SS Pol. Gebietsfuehrer Kamenez reports that on the 23rd in cooperation with the security services a Jew-operation was carried out in Stara-Utschitza (Uzice) and Studenica...700, being incapable of work, were shot," read one report.
The Germans did not limit themselves to killing Jews, for dictator Adolf Hitler regarded all those living in the Soviet Union as subhumans.
One partially decoded message showed a commander in Belarus boasting in August 1941 that "the figure of executions carried out in my area now exceeds the 30,000 mark".
British intelligence commented laconically:

"The tone of this message suggests that the word has gone out that a definite decrease in the total population of Russia would be welcomed in high quarters and that the leaders of the three sectors (of that particular front) stand somewhat in competition with each other as to their 'score.'"
By the very end of October the Nazi forces were wreaking havoc in the Ukrainian city of Kremenchug, or Krementschug as it was known in German.
"There is every indication that in Krementschug the 'action according to the usage of war'...was on a scale exceeding even the previous brutality of the German police," said the report.

"The special section in charge of the job (ask local commander) Jeckeln for his permission to start. At 2230 on the 30th he gives it, and we may suppose that the butchery went on all through the night."
